newsitem.title: USA: Brazil trade gap not forcing tighter policy - Loyola.
newsitem.headline: Brazil trade gap not forcing tighter policy - Loyola.

text.p: Brazil can finance its burgeoning trade deficit through investment, and will not need to rein in economic growth in pursuit of current accounts improvement, the country's central banker said Friday.
Gustavo Loyola, president of the Brazil's central bank, said there were no plans to alter monetary policy or change the pace of currency depreciation.
"This trade deficit can be financed easily through direct investment or long-term capital," Loyola told reporters after a conference here.
Loyola vowed to stay the "stay the course" of lowering domestic interest rates and gradually allowing the real to depreciate with its band system.
"We don't see any need to reduce the pace of the current growth," he said. "I don't see any need for a change in exchange rate policy."
Brazil posted a $655 million trade gap in September and Brazilian economists believed the deficit could widen another $1.0 billion in October to reach $4.0 billion by year end.
Loyola pegged this year's current account deficit at about three percent of GDP, and forecast the same level for 1997, and added that the trade performance was actually "very good."
"Exports are growing at a very good pace, 5-6 percent per year," he said.
He reaffirmed the country's commitment to foreign bond issuance to pay down some of its heavy domestic debt burden, but offered no timetable of when this would take place.
Brazil was continuing to study Brady bond buyback plans, but no decision has been made, Loyola said.
